item.content:encoded:
This day in Los Angeles Dodgers history saw the end of an era at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, plus Sandy Koufax and Clayton Kershaw reach individual milestones.
On Sept. 20, 1961, the Dodgers came away with a 3-2 walk-off win against the Chicago Cubs in 13 innings. The game was notable in that Koufax not only pitched all 13 innings but it was the Dodgers’ final time playing at the L.A. Coliseum.
It was their home since moving from Brooklyn for the start of the 1958 season and until Dodger Stadium opened on April 10, 1962.
En route to pitching a complete game, Koufax finished with 15 strikeouts to earn his 18th win of the season.
Although that marked the Dodgers’ final time playing at the Coliseum, their 1961 season concluded with a nine-game road trip comprised of series against the St. Louis Cardinals, Pittsburgh Pirates and Cubs.
The Dodgers went 89-65, good for second place in the National League. They finished four games back of the Cincinnati Reds, who lost in the World Series to the New York Yankees.
On Sept. 20, 1966, Koufax was part of another memorable performance as he became the first NL pitcher in 31 years with back-to-back seasons of at least 25 victories.
Koufax reached the milestone with a complete game in the Dodgers 11-1 win over the Philadelphia Phillies at Dodger Stadium. The left-hander had 26 wins in 1965 and 27 in 1966, which wound up being his final season.
On Sept. 20, 2011, Kershaw became the Dodgers’ first 20-game winner since Ramon Martinez accomplished the feat in 1990. Kershaw pitched 7.1 innings against the San Francisco Giants to earn his 20th win.
Dodgers returned to Coliseum
On March 29, 2008, the Dodgers faced defending World Series champion Boston Red Sox in front of 115,300 fans for an exhibition game at the L.A. Memorial Coliseum. It was held to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Dodgers franchise moving from Brooklyn to Los Angeles.
The crowd represented the largest ever for a baseball game, surpassing the approximately 114,000 fans that were in attendance when the Australian national team played an American services team during the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne.

item.content:encoded:
“Sandy would strike me out two or three times a game. I knew every pitch he was going to throw, and I still could not hit him.” — Willie Mays, Hall of Fame outfielder
Short versions of the meaning of the word dominator would be someone of importance who has authority or control, or who rules over a situation.
The list is long and too many to name, but the major league pitchers who were in complete control during a game would have to include the Dodgers’ crafty left-handed Hall of Famer, Sandy Koufax.
Koufax is the youngest man ever inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame, at the age of 36 in 1972. He was only the second Jewish player ever to be inducted.
Not the official list, but my first reaction would be to place Nolan Ryan and Randy Johnson right at the top, and Bob Gibson would be in my threesome. Can you imagine how hard it was to hit any of those three guys? Where would you place Tom Seaver, Steve Carlton and Don Sutton? Maybe put them in your lineup with Justin Verlander, Max Scherzer and Gaylord Perry. What about Walter Johnson, Clayton Kershaw, Cy Young, Jim Bunning and Greg Maddux? Can’t leave them off. There are others, and I am reminded of the World War II era patriots, Bob Feller and Warren Spahn.
The Dodgers franchise officials would have been smiling if they had known that on Dec. 30th, 1935, not far from Ebbets Field in Brooklyn, a future phenom pitcher was born. A Brooklyn native he was, and destiny saw to it that Mr. Koufax would become a name associated with Dodger successes, feted as one of the greatest pitchers of all time.
He was born with the name Sanford Braun, with the last name Koufax being added as he was named after his stepfather. Sandy is the name he used and is recorded in most written accounts of this great icon.
Sandy Koufax never played in the minor leagues, as he started with the Brooklyn Dodgers at age 19 in 1955. Fate was with him from the start, as this was the storybook team that beat the Yankees in the World Series. There were a few other names that never played in the lower leagues. Consider Mel Ott, Al Kaline, Ernie Banks, Catfish Hunter and Dick Groat. There are others.
Koufax teamed up with Don Drysdale, and they became an unbeatable team on and off the field. By that I mean working together on TV, doing commercials, special events and Dodger promotions, magazine and newspaper articles; they were household names. They even teamed up as a pair of holdouts one year to try to get the Dodgers to raise their salaries. My guess is that before the players’ union, they were very limited as to how much leverage they could muster against the dictatorial management of Major League Baseball.
Sandy attended Columbia University after high school and later the University of Cincinnati with the intention of becoming an architect. Ironically, his path led him to baseball, and now his choice to play “America’s Game’ was good for baseball and especially the fans. He started playing in local leagues around New York City. While in school playing basketball for the University of Cincinnati, he was recruited by the baseball team. Boy, if that baseball coach had only known how his choosing Sandy to play for him would affect Major League Baseball history.
Koufax only pitched 12 seasons in the big leagues, all with the Dodgers, and retired because of arm trouble. With sports medicine as it is today, he may have been able to pitch longer with modern arm treatments and protocols.
Starting in Brooklyn in 1955, he pitched through 1966, ending the majority of his years with the L.A. Dodgers. In 397 games, he posted a record of 165 wins and 87 losses, logging an amazing .655 winning percentage. He fanned 2,396 batters and only walked 817.
Sandy made the All-Star team seven times and was the National League MVP in 1963. He captured the Cy Young Award three times and was a two-time World Series MVP. He was on four World Championship Dodgers teams: 1955, ’59, ’63, and ’65. He was the National League strikeout leader four times. He had four no-hitters and one perfect game. On Sept. 9, 1965, at Dodger Stadium, he pitched a perfect game against the Chicago Cubs. Incidentally, the losing pitcher for the Cubs was Bob Hendley, a native of Macon, Ga., and a standout hurler for Lanier High School in Macon back in the 1950s.
Sandy Koufax’s jersey No. 32 is retired by the Dodgers. He is recognized as a member of Major League Baseball's All-Time Team, the All-Century Team, and, of course, the Hall of Fame. Sandy is soon to be 91 years old and is active as a supporter and a goodwill ambassador for the Dodgers and baseball in general. He was the best of the best.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have a long line of notable pitchers and on this day in franchise history, those stars shined a little brighter throughout the years.
On Sept. 17, 1963, Sandy Koufax pitched a shutout against the St. Louis Cardinals at Sportsman’s Park while giving up just four hits.
The shutout was his 11th of the season, which set a new National League record for the most in one year by a left-hander in MLB history. Grover Cleveland Alexander held the Major League Record with 16 shutouts during the 1916 season for the Philadelphia Phillies.
Also on this day in Dodgers history but during the 1981 season, Fernando Valenzuela threw his eighth shutout of the year with a three-hitter against the Atlanta Braves.
With eight shutouts, Valenzuela tied the rookie record that was set by Chicago White Sox pitcher Ewell Russell in 1913. In addition, Valenzuela broke the previous NL mark shared by Irving Young (Boston Beaneaters, 1905), Grover Cleveland Alexander (Phillies, 1911), and Jerry Koosman (New York Mets, 1968).
Dodgers history: Sept. 17
Nomo no-hitter
In 1996, 15 years after Valenzuela and 33 years after Koufax set their shutout records, Hideo Nomo threw the only no-hitter in history at Coors Field. It was one of two Nomo tossed during his 12-year career.
Nomo’s historic game came with the club locked in a pennant race and it was the 20th no-hitter in franchise history.
Joe Torre retires
Also on this day in Dodgers history, manager Joe Torre announced he will retire following the end of the 2010 season. He finished his career with a record of 2326-1997 (.538) during his 30 seasons as a skipper with Mets, Braves, Cardinals, New York Yankees, and the Dodgers.
The Dodgers then announced the team’s hitting coach Don Mattingly was hired to replace Torre, who accepted a position to assist Major League Baseball Commissioner Bud Selig as the new Executive Vice President for Baseball Operations.
